text.p: Israeli leaders have long found a way to come back from the depths of scandal.
Israel's attorney general on Sunday said no charges would be filed against Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu over an influence-peddling scandal though some of his associates could still be indicted.

In 1983 a state inquiry found two members of Netanyahu's own current cabinet, Ariel Sharon and Rafael Eitan, indirectly responsible for the 1982 massacre of Palestinians by Christian militiamen at two Beirut refugee camps surrounded by Israeli soldiers.

Sharon, a member of Netanyahu's Likud party, was forced to resign as defence minister and Eitan was reprimanded as army chief of staff but both went on to serve as cabinet ministers in successive governments.

In 1984 Israel's Shin Bet security service tried to frame another future Likud leader, Defence Minister Yitzhak Mordechai, for the killing by Shin Bet agents of two Palestinian bus hijackers in custody.
Mordechai, then an army commander, was exonerated with the revelation of a Shin Bet cover-up. Those involved were later granted presidential immunity from prosecution.

Rabbi Aryeh Deri, a former interior minister at the centre of the latest allegations, represents the ultra-religious Jewish Shas party in parliament despite being on trial in another corruption scandal.
The last time a scandal toppled a government was in 1977 when prime minister Yitzhak Rabin's wife Leah was discovered to have had a U.S. bank account, then illegal in Israel.
Rabin, a former ambassador to Washington, was not charged but resigned anyway.
He remained a leader of the left-centre Labour party and went on to serve as prime minister from 1992 until his assassination in November 1995.
